what: Hagerty insures classic and collector cars. It writes specialist policies that value a vehicle at an agreed collector price rather than depreciated book value, and surrounds that with a membership club, valuation data, auctions, events and a magazine for people who own old cars.
customers: Owners of classic, collector and enthusiast vehicles in the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom, plus the broader community of enthusiasts who engage with its media and events.
money: Commissions on insurance policies placed with carrier partners.
Premium retained through its own underwriting entity.
Club memberships, auction revenue, events and media.
moat: Insuring a classic car requires knowing what it is worth, which depends on decades of auction and sale data that Hagerty has accumulated and competitors have not. Collector cars are also driven rarely and cared for obsessively, so the claims experience is far better than ordinary motor insurance — a pricing advantage that only holds if you understand the risk, which requires the same data.
risks: Reported net income of $60.1M produces a price/earnings ratio of 270, because the corporate structure means only part of the income accrues to the listed shares — the earnings multiple is therefore not comparable to a normal company’s.
EV/EBITDA of 52.1 is a very high multiple whichever way the earnings are allocated.
Eight analysts average a $17.13 target, only 6% above the current price.
A classic car is a discretionary asset, and both insurance renewals and auction activity weaken when collectors feel poorer.
Growth has partly come from expanding into ordinary enthusiast vehicles, where the claims advantage and the data moat are both weaker.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $619.1M in 2021 to $1.5B in 2025.
Free cash flow of $279.6M on $1.4B of revenue is strong, and the shares trade at about 19.9 times it.
Decades of valuation data on collector vehicles is a genuine asset that cannot be assembled retrospectively.
Collector cars are driven rarely and maintained carefully, which produces far better claims experience than ordinary motor insurance.
The membership, media and auction businesses create a community that makes the insurance relationship unusually durable.
watch: Policies in force and the retention rate. This is a membership business as much as an insurance one, and renewal behaviour tells you whether the community is real.
view: Hagerty has built something unusual: an insurance company that functions as a club. Members get a policy, but they also get a magazine, valuation tools, events, auctions and a sense of belonging to the collector car world. That matters commercially because it makes the insurance relationship stickier than price comparison would allow — a member renewing is renewing a membership, not shopping a policy.

Underneath the community is a genuine data asset. Insuring a classic car requires knowing what it is worth, which is not a book value calculation but a judgement built from decades of auction results and private sales. Hagerty has that history and competitors do not, and it cannot be assembled retrospectively. The data also underpins the underwriting advantage: collector cars are driven rarely and maintained obsessively, so claims experience is far better than ordinary motor insurance — but that advantage only works if you can price the risk, which requires the data.

The reported earnings need care. A price/earnings ratio of 270 on $60 million of net income reflects a corporate structure where only part of the income accrues to the listed shares, so the multiple is not comparable to an ordinary company’s. The honest figures are $280 million of free cash flow at about 19.9 times, and 52 times EV/EBITDA, which is a very high price however the earnings are divided.

What gives me pause is the direction of the growth. Revenue has more than doubled to $1.5 billion, partly by expanding beyond true classics into ordinary enthusiast vehicles — modified cars, newer sports cars, general enthusiast policies. That is a much larger market, and it is also one where the claims advantage is weaker and the valuation data moat barely applies. Growing into a market where your moat does not reach is how specialist insurers become ordinary ones. Eight analysts seeing 6% of upside suggests the market has noticed. Policies in force and retention are the figures that reveal whether the club is still a club.
bull: The membership model and irreplaceable valuation data keep retention exceptionally high while the enthusiast market expands the addressable base several times over.
bear: Expansion into ordinary enthusiast vehicles dilutes both the claims advantage and the data moat, discretionary collector spending weakens, and a 52 times EV/EBITDA multiple contracts.
